options.a: Connect the first trailer directly to the tractor
options.b: Couple a second trailer to the first
options.c: Supply trailer air in place of glad hands
options.d: Lower the rig's center of gravity

distractorExplanations.a: The first trailer couples to the tractor's fifth wheel by its kingpin; the dolly is needed only to support the front of the second or third trailer.
distractorExplanations.c: Air reaches the rear trailer through the dolly's hoses and glad hands; the dolly is a coupling device, not a replacement for air connections.
distractorExplanations.d: A dolly adds an articulation point and does nothing to lower the center of gravity; doubles are actually more rollover-prone at the rear.

options.a: The pintle hook alone, without chains
options.b: Fifth-wheel jaws locked around the dolly kingpin
options.c: Pintle/eye and safety devices as designed
options.d: Air lines first, then the pintle latch later

distractorExplanations.a: Safety chains/cables are required back-up connections; relying on the pintle hook alone leaves nothing to hold the dolly if the eye fails.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the two coupling points: the dolly tongue eye goes into the first trailer's pintle hook; fifth-wheel jaws lock the second trailer's kingpin.
distractorExplanations.d: Sequence error: the mechanical pintle/eye connection and safety chains are secured before the air and electrical lines are connected.

options.a: Release the second trailer's spring brakes first
options.b: Raise the trailer nose well above the fifth wheel
options.c: Connect the rear trailer's air and light lines
options.d: Align carefully; chock as required; check heights

distractorExplanations.a: The second trailer's brakes stay set (or wheels chocked) so it cannot roll away while the dolly is pushed under it; releasing them comes later.
distractorExplanations.b: The trailer nose should sit slightly lower than the center of the dolly fifth wheel so it lifts a little as the dolly slides under; too high risks a high hitch.
distractorExplanations.c: Air and electrical lines are connected after the mechanical coupling is made and tested, not before backing the dolly under the trailer.

options.a: Run straight to the pintle so they stay clear in tight turns
options.b: Pulled tight with no slack so the tongue cannot move
options.c: Crossed/secured per design so trailer is held if eye fails
options.d: Hooked to the landing gear of the second trailer

distractorExplanations.a: Chains are crossed under the tongue to cradle it if the eye or pintle fails; straight chains let the tongue drop to the road.
distractorExplanations.b: Chains need enough slack to allow turning; drawn taut they can bind or break in a turn and still fail in their back-up role.
distractorExplanations.d: Dolly safety chains attach to the towing (first) trailer's chain points near the pintle hook, not to the second trailer's landing gear.

options.a: Connected before the pintle and kingpin are locked
options.b: Hooked up with rear shut-offs closed
options.c: Connected through dolly lines correctly
options.d: Run straight from the tractor, bypassing the dolly

distractorExplanations.a: Lines are hooked up after the mechanical coupling is made and tested; connecting them first risks damaged hoses if the trailer moves.
distractorExplanations.b: The shut-off valves at the rear of the first trailer must be opened to pass air back; closed valves leave the rear trailer without service or emergency air.
distractorExplanations.d: The rear trailer gets air and power through the first trailer and the dolly's hoses and cord, not through a separate line from the tractor.

options.a: Overloading the tractor's steer axle
options.b: Tripping the tractor protection valve
options.c: A trailer ABS fault
options.d: Poor coupling/damage

distractorExplanations.a: Dolly fifth-wheel height affects the second trailer's coupling, not the tractor steer-axle load, which depends on the first trailer's kingpin weight.
distractorExplanations.b: The tractor protection valve responds to low air pressure or a broken trailer line, not to a height mismatch between dolly and trailer.
distractorExplanations.c: A height mismatch causes a high hitch or bumped apron, a mechanical coupling problem; ABS faults come from sensors, wiring or power supply.

options.a: Release that trailer's brakes so it can be towed
options.b: Apply that trailer’s spring brakes / protect system as designed
options.c: Affect the service brakes only, leaving parking brakes off
options.d: Have no effect until the tractor air drops below 20 psi

distractorExplanations.a: Loss of emergency (supply) air makes the trailer's emergency/spring brakes apply; it does not release them.
distractorExplanations.c: Emergency-line loss triggers the trailer emergency/spring brakes; the effect is not limited to the service brake circuit.
distractorExplanations.d: The trailer reacts as soon as its emergency line pressure is lost; the 20–45 psi range describes when the tractor protection valve closes, not a delay.

options.a: Tires, lights, pintle, air lines, suspension
options.b: Air lines and glad hands; tires are checked at the shop
options.c: The dolly tongue and eye, since it carries no brakes
options.d: Lights and reflectors, since it bears little weight

distractorExplanations.b: Dolly tires, wheels and suspension are part of the driver's pre-trip inspection; they are not deferred to shop maintenance.
distractorExplanations.c: Converter dollies have their own brakes and air tank; checking just the tongue and eye skips brakes, tires and lights.
distractorExplanations.d: Lighting is part of it, but a dolly carries the second trailer's nose weight and needs tires, pintle/eye, chains, air lines and suspension checked.

options.a: Loss of air pressure in the dolly's tank
options.b: The need to cross the safety chains
options.c: Overloading the first trailer's rear axle
options.d: Damage and unsafe angles during couple

distractorExplanations.a: Tongue support is mechanical; dolly air pressure depends on lines, valves and the reservoir drain, not on how the tongue is propped.
distractorExplanations.b: Tongue support does not replace safety chains; crossed chains are still required to catch the tongue if the eye or pintle fails.
distractorExplanations.c: Axle loading comes from the second trailer's weight on the dolly, not from how the tongue is held while coupling.

options.a: Tug tests are unsafe with doubles
options.b: Dolly kingpins cannot be inspected visually
options.c: The jaws lock only when air is connected
options.d: You must verify each connection

distractorExplanations.a: A tug test in low gear against the locked trailer brakes is the standard coupling check for doubles as well as singles.
distractorExplanations.b: You can and must look to confirm the fifth-wheel jaws are closed around the kingpin shank and the locking lever is in the locked position.
distractorExplanations.c: Fifth-wheel jaws lock mechanically when the kingpin enters; connecting air does not lock them, so air hookup proves nothing about the coupling.

options.a: Show clearance lamps, with tail and stop on the dolly
options.b: Be checked only before night driving
options.c: Be wired through the tractor directly, not the dolly
options.d: Display required tail/stop/turn/clearance

distractorExplanations.a: Tail, stop and turn lamps must be on the rear of the last trailer where following traffic sees them, not on the dolly ahead of it.
distractorExplanations.b: Stop and turn signals operate day and night; every required rear lamp is checked on each pre-trip, not just before night driving.
distractorExplanations.c: Rear-trailer lighting is fed through the first trailer's rear receptacle and the dolly's cord, not a separate circuit from the tractor.

options.a: Tractor jackknife before the trailers react
options.b: Rear trailer swing/rollover
options.c: The first trailer to roll before the rear
options.d: Sway the dolly absorbs

distractorExplanations.a: Tractor jackknife results from drive-wheel lockup under braking; a sudden steering input is amplified at the last trailer (crack-the-whip).
distractorExplanations.c: Rearward amplification makes the rear trailer the most likely to roll over, not the trailer directly behind the tractor.
distractorExplanations.d: A converter dolly adds an articulation point that amplifies sway toward the rear; it does not damp or absorb it.

options.a: Possible with mirrors if the dolly is locked straight
options.b: Much harder—avoid when possible; get help
options.c: Like backing a single, but with smaller steering inputs
options.d: Fine if you steer toward the drift

distractorExplanations.a: Converter dollies pivot at the pintle, so a doubles combination cannot be reliably backed even with careful mirror use; plan to avoid backing.
distractorExplanations.c: Smaller inputs do not make it like a single: the extra pivot makes the rear trailer react unpredictably, so routes are planned to avoid backing.
distractorExplanations.d: Steering toward the drift is the single-trailer technique; with two pivot points the rear trailer jackknifes quickly, so doubles should not be backed.

options.a: Eliminated by the dolly's pivot point
options.b: Toward the outside of the curve at low speed
options.c: More complex—plan wider turns
options.d: Fixed by an early turn-in

distractorExplanations.a: The dolly adds an articulation point, but the rear trailer still tracks inside the tractor's path, so off-tracking must be planned for.
distractorExplanations.b: At low speed trailers off-track to the inside of the turn; outward off-tracking occurs at higher speeds, so the low-speed direction is reversed.
distractorExplanations.d: Turning in early drags the rear wheels over the inside curb; you must go forward farther and swing wide as needed.

options.a: Straight grades once the trailers start to sway
options.b: Curves, ramps, and lane changes
options.c: Midway through each curve
options.d: Merges only; ramps are built for truck speed

distractorExplanations.a: Slowing after sway begins is too late; speed is reduced before curves and ramps, where the rear trailer is most prone to roll.
distractorExplanations.c: Braking in the curve shifts weight and invites swing; speed must come off before the curve or ramp, not while in it.
distractorExplanations.d: Ramp advisory speeds are set for cars and can be too fast for a high-CG double; slow down well below posted ramp speeds.

options.a: More stable than loaded ones
options.b: Less affected by crosswinds
options.c: Slow to wheel lockup
options.d: Light and swing-prone

distractorExplanations.a: Empty or light trailers bounce and swing more readily; the heavier trailer belongs up front to stabilize the combination.
distractorExplanations.b: A light trailer with large sides is pushed more easily, so crosswinds affect an empty rear trailer more, not less.
distractorExplanations.c: Lightly loaded axles lock up more easily under braking because there is less weight on the tires, which raises skid risk.

options.a: Matter mainly on the lead trailer
options.b: Are offset by keeping speed up
options.c: Are managed by quick steering
options.d: Can push rear units—slow down

distractorExplanations.a: Crosswinds hit the whole combination, but the light rear trailer is the unit most easily pushed out of its lane.
distractorExplanations.b: Higher speed magnifies wind-induced sway; the correct response to strong crosswinds is to slow down or park.
distractorExplanations.c: Quick corrections amplify sway at the rear trailer; use smooth, small steering inputs and reduce speed instead.

options.a: ABS on the dolly delays brake application
options.b: Air reaches the rear trailer brakes first
options.c: Stopping distance and stability margins are tighter
options.d: Engine braking is unavailable with a converter dolly

distractorExplanations.a: ABS prevents wheel lockup; it does not delay brake application. The longer stop comes from extra weight and air travel time.
distractorExplanations.b: Air brake lag is greatest at the rear trailer, which is farthest from the treadle valve; rear brakes apply last, not first.
distractorExplanations.d: Engine and retarder braking still work with doubles; braking early is needed because of greater mass and longer stopping distance.

options.a: Signal early, then move quickly to limit exposure
options.b: Check the lead trailer, then cut in once it clears
options.c: Move gradually, signaling once the lane change starts
options.d: Signal early, move gradually, watch rear trailer

distractorExplanations.a: A quick move whips the rear trailer (rearward amplification); lane changes with doubles must be slow and gradual.
distractorExplanations.b: Clearance is judged by the rear trailer, the last unit to enter the lane; cutting in once the lead trailer clears can strike the vehicle beside it.
distractorExplanations.c: Signals go on well before moving so others can react; signaling only after the move begins gives no warning.

options.a: Firm braking in curves to settle the trailers
options.b: Smooth inputs; proper brake function; sane speed
options.c: Quick steering corrections at the first sign of drift
options.d: Using the trailer hand valve to stop in curves

distractorExplanations.a: Braking in a curve shifts weight and can lock the light rear axles; slow down before the curve and keep inputs smooth.
distractorExplanations.c: Quick corrections are amplified at the last trailer and can start the swing; small, smooth steering inputs are needed.
distractorExplanations.d: The trailer hand valve applies trailer brakes alone and can lock trailer wheels; it is not used for routine or curve braking.

options.a: Use a higher gear and brake steadily to the bottom
options.b: Light, continuous braking keeps the brakes cool
options.c: Gear selection and heat management are critical
options.d: Downshift once the speed reaches the safe limit

distractorExplanations.a: A high gear forces continuous braking that overheats and fades the brakes; choose a low gear before the grade and use snub braking.
distractorExplanations.b: Continuous light pressure builds heat; manuals teach snub braking—brake to about 5 mph below safe speed, release, repeat.
distractorExplanations.d: Shifting down after speed builds is too late and can leave you stuck in neutral; select the low gear before starting down.

options.a: Same as a single trailer of equal length
options.b: Increased vs singles/cars
options.c: One second per 20 feet of length
options.d: Shorter with ABS

distractorExplanations.a: Doubles need extra space beyond a single because rear-trailer swing and greater weight lengthen a safe stop.
distractorExplanations.c: The manual rule is one second per 10 feet of vehicle length below 40 mph, plus one second above 40; per 20 feet halves the gap.
distractorExplanations.d: ABS keeps steering control during hard braking but does not shorten stopping distance enough to justify a smaller gap.

options.a: Brake hard to pull the rear trailer back into line
options.b: Apply the trailer hand valve to straighten the trailers
options.c: Steer sharply against the swing to stop it quickly
options.d: Ease controls; do not brake harshly if it worsens swing

distractorExplanations.a: Hard braking can lock the light rear trailer's wheels and worsen the swing; braking is eased off, not increased.
distractorExplanations.b: Applying trailer brakes alone can lock the trailer wheels and make the swing worse; the hand valve is not a recovery tool.
distractorExplanations.c: Sharp counter-steering is amplified at the rear and can roll the last trailer; use smooth, measured steering.

options.a: Stable once the lead trailer is loaded
options.b: A rollover/swing recipe
options.c: A setup ABS fully corrects
options.d: Fine at speeds under 65 mph

distractorExplanations.a: A heavy lead trailer helps, but a light rear trailer at speed still swings and rolls easily (crack-the-whip effect).
distractorExplanations.c: ABS prevents wheel lockup under braking; it does not stop rearward amplification or rollover caused by speed and steering.
distractorExplanations.d: No fixed speed makes a light rear trailer safe; rollover risk rises with speed and steering inputs, so slow below posted limits.

options.a: Is done by backing both trailers in one pass
options.b: Often requires special spotting/setup
options.c: Is like a single: cut the corner
options.d: Needs only mirrors, since spotters add confusion

distractorExplanations.a: Backing doubles into a dock is impractical because the dolly pivot makes the rear trailer jackknife; trailers are dropped and spotted instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Cutting the corner drags the trailers' inside wheels across curbs and objects; doubles need planned, wide approaches.
distractorExplanations.d: Mirrors leave large blind areas around a double; a spotter with agreed signals is recommended in tight spaces.

options.a: One unit, checked from the tractor end
options.b: Separate vehicles with full checks
options.c: Full checks on the lead trailer, spot checks after
options.d: Separate units except dolly brakes

distractorExplanations.a: Each trailer and the dolly has its own brakes, tires, lights and couplings and must be inspected separately, not as one unit.
distractorExplanations.c: The rear trailer and dolly need the same full inspection as the first; spot-checking them misses defects where swing risk is highest.
distractorExplanations.d: Converter dollies have brakes and an air tank that must be checked; skipping them leaves the rear coupling's braking unverified.

options.a: Matched to the tractor's steer tires
options.b: Inflated to the sidewall's minimum
options.c: Inflated and undamaged
options.d: Free of tread rules

distractorExplanations.a: Dolly tires must be properly inflated and free of cuts or bulges; there is no rule that they match the steer tires.
distractorExplanations.b: The sidewall shows the maximum pressure at maximum load; correct inflation follows the load chart, not a minimum figure.
distractorExplanations.d: Dolly tires fall under the same tread and damage rules as other trailer tires (2/32 inch minimum on non-steer tires).

options.a: Paint condition and stamped rating
options.b: Air leaks at the pintle hook
options.c: Jaw closure on the eye
options.d: Cracks, wear, secure latch

distractorExplanations.a: A rating stamp matters, but the pre-trip check looks for cracks, excessive wear and a properly closed, locked latch.
distractorExplanations.b: The pintle hook is a mechanical coupler with no air connection; air leaks are checked at the glad hands and hoses.
distractorExplanations.c: Jaws belong to the fifth-wheel coupling; the pintle/eye check covers the hook, the eye, the latch and its lock pin.

options.a: Stays on while driving
options.b: Clear by restart
options.c: Note faults
options.d: Signals low air

distractorExplanations.a: The trailer ABS lamp should come on briefly at start-up and then go out; staying lit while moving signals an ABS fault to report.
distractorExplanations.b: Cycling the ignition may turn the lamp off, but the fault still needs to be noted and repaired; a restart does not fix it.
distractorExplanations.d: Low air pressure is shown by the low-air warning light or buzzer at about 60 psi, not by the trailer ABS lamp.

options.a: Wheel chocks in place of chains
options.b: One chain, attached at the center
options.c: Landing-gear pins only
options.d: Chains/cables as required

distractorExplanations.a: Wheel chocks secure a parked trailer; they do not replace the safety chains that hold the dolly if the eye fails.
distractorExplanations.b: Dollies use a pair of chains crossed under the tongue; a single center chain gives no cradle if the eye breaks.
distractorExplanations.c: Landing gear belongs to semitrailers; the dolly's required safety devices are its chains or cables to the towing trailer.

options.a: Check tractor axles; trailers at service
options.b: Tractor slack only
options.c: Inspect like any CDL unit
options.d: Inspect at the annual DOT check

distractorExplanations.a: Trailer and dolly axles are inspected by the driver on every pre-trip, not deferred to scheduled service.
distractorExplanations.b: Brake adjustment must be checked on every axle, including both trailers and the dolly, not just on the tractor.
distractorExplanations.d: The annual inspection does not replace the daily pre-trip; suspension and brakes are checked before every trip.

options.a: Tractor and rear trailer lamps work
options.b: Rear lamps work on the lead trailer
options.c: All required lamps function
options.d: Tractor signals flash

distractorExplanations.a: The first trailer and dolly lamps (clearance, marker, side) must work too; checking only the two ends skips the middle units.
distractorExplanations.b: Stop and tail lamps must work at the very rear; the lead trailer's rear lamps are hidden by the dolly and second trailer.
distractorExplanations.d: Tractor turn signals alone do not prove the signal circuit reaches the rear trailer through the dolly cord.

options.a: Reinspect coupling/lines/lights before rolling
options.b: Reinspect lights; couplings are already tested
options.c: Tug-test the coupling and depart without line checks
options.d: Reinspect at the next scheduled stop

distractorExplanations.b: Each new coupling must be checked and tug-tested again; earlier tests do not cover a reconfigured combination.
distractorExplanations.c: A tug test checks the mechanical coupling but not the air and electrical lines; brakes and lights at the rear must be verified too.
distractorExplanations.d: Problems from re-coupling must be found before moving; the next stop could be too late for an unlocked pintle or crossed lines.

options.a: Present and intact
options.b: Raised at speed
options.c: Required on the tractor only
options.d: Checked at annual inspection

distractorExplanations.b: Mudflaps/splash guards stay down to control road spray; raising or removing them is not allowed where they are required.
distractorExplanations.c: Splash guards are required behind the rear wheels of trailers too where state rules call for them, not just on the tractor.
distractorExplanations.d: Mudflaps and their securing hardware are part of each pre-trip walk-around, not left to the annual inspection.

options.a: Fix before dispatch
options.b: Fix at the next service
options.c: Normal if pressure builds
options.d: Drain the tank

distractorExplanations.b: A leaking air-ride bag can drop the dolly's ride height and affect coupling and braking; it is fixed before dispatch, not deferred.
distractorExplanations.c: Building pressure does not make a leak acceptable; a leaking air bag is a defect even if the compressor keeps up with it.
distractorExplanations.d: Draining the dolly air tank removes moisture but does nothing to repair a leaking air bag; the leak itself must be fixed.

options.a: Can kill lights/ABS—clean/repair
options.b: Affects lights but not trailer ABS
options.c: Is cleared by reseating the plug
options.d: Matters only in wet weather

distractorExplanations.b: Trailer ABS is powered through the same seven-way connector, so corrosion can cause ABS faults as well as lighting failures.
distractorExplanations.c: Reseating may restore contact briefly, but corroded pins must be cleaned or replaced to prevent intermittent failures.
distractorExplanations.d: Corrosion raises resistance in dry conditions too and can cause dim or dead lamps at any time; it is repaired, not ignored.

options.a: Full tractor-trailer couple checks
options.b: A pintle-hook latch check
options.c: A tug test, with no visual check
options.d: Checks only if the trailer was dropped

distractorExplanations.b: The pintle hook belongs to the dolly connection; the tractor-to-first-trailer link needs kingpin and fifth-wheel checks.
distractorExplanations.c: Both are required: a tug test plus a visual check that the jaws close around the kingpin shank and the release arm is locked.
distractorExplanations.d: The fifth wheel and kingpin are checked on every pre-trip, not only after a trailer has been dropped and re-coupled.

options.a: Report them after the trip ends
options.b: Do not operate unsafe equipment
options.c: Note them; drive if under 100 miles
options.d: Record them for the annual check

distractorExplanations.a: Safety defects found before the trip are reported and repaired before driving; a post-trip report does not cover operating with a known defect.
distractorExplanations.c: There is no short-trip exception; equipment with safety defects must not be operated until it is repaired.
distractorExplanations.d: Defects affecting safety are repaired before operation; the annual inspection is not where daily defects wait.

options.a: Rearward amplification / swing
options.b: Jackknife of the lead trailer
options.c: Brake lag at the tractor axle
options.d: Overloading the steer axle

distractorExplanations.b: The typical doubles hazard is the rear trailer amplifying steering inputs (crack-the-whip), not the first trailer jackknifing.
distractorExplanations.c: Air brake lag is greatest at the rear trailer, farthest from the treadle valve, not at the tractor axle.
distractorExplanations.d: Steer-axle load depends on kingpin weight and placement; the defining doubles hazard is rear-trailer swing and rollover.

options.a: Bridges, not curves or ramps
options.b: Curves, exits, and merges
options.c: The middle of each curve
options.d: Merges, then speed up in curves

distractorExplanations.a: Curves, ramps and merges are where doubles roll over; slowing for bridges alone ignores the main rollover points.
distractorExplanations.c: Speed must come off before entering the curve; braking mid-curve shifts weight and can trigger swing or wheel lockup.
distractorExplanations.d: Accelerating or holding speed in curves increases lateral force and rollover risk for the rear trailer.

options.a: Heavier than the lead trailer's load
options.b: Secured; understand empty/light behavior
options.c: Loaded to the rear doors for traction
options.d: Secured once, at the shipper's dock

distractorExplanations.a: The heavier trailer goes first, directly behind the tractor; a heavier rear trailer increases swing and rollover risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Weight is distributed to keep axle loads legal and the center of gravity low; piling it at the doors overloads the rear axle.
distractorExplanations.d: Securement is rechecked within the first 50 miles and then every 3 hours or 150 miles en route, not just once at the dock.

options.a: Firm control; allow ABS to work; watch combination behavior
options.b: Pump the brakes to keep the ABS from cycling
options.c: Use the trailer hand valve first to keep trailers straight
options.d: Shift to neutral first, then brake with full force

distractorExplanations.b: With ABS you hold firm, steady pressure; pumping the pedal defeats the system and lengthens the stop.
distractorExplanations.c: Applying trailer brakes first can lock the trailer wheels and cause swing; the hand valve is not for emergency stopping.
distractorExplanations.d: Neutral removes engine braking and some control; stay in gear and brake firmly, letting ABS prevent wheel lockup.

options.a: Same as a single
options.b: Bigger than you think
options.c: Smaller with dual-trailer ABS
options.d: Ahead only; sides matter less

distractorExplanations.a: Doubles need more space than a single because of added weight, rear-trailer swing and brake lag at the last trailer.
distractorExplanations.c: ABS keeps steering control but does not shorten stopping distance enough to justify a smaller space cushion.
distractorExplanations.d: A space cushion is managed ahead, behind and on both sides, since rear-trailer swing can move into adjacent lanes.

options.a: Mainly at low speed in tight yards
options.b: Unless the rear trailer is loaded heavy
options.c: Especially at speed with multiple trailers
options.d: Except when swerving around a hazard at speed

distractorExplanations.a: Abrupt steering is most dangerous at highway speed, where rearward amplification can roll the last trailer.
distractorExplanations.b: A loaded rear trailer does not cancel swing risk; heavy-rear setups are themselves discouraged, and sharp inputs stay dangerous.
distractorExplanations.d: Swerving at speed is exactly when sudden steering can whip and overturn the rear trailer; smooth, controlled inputs are needed.

options.a: Plan early; manage brake heat
options.b: Coast in neutral to save the brakes
options.c: Use light, steady brake pressure
options.d: Downshift once speed builds

distractorExplanations.b: Coasting in neutral removes engine braking and is illegal in many states; it forces the service brakes to do all the work.
distractorExplanations.c: Steady light braking builds heat and fades the brakes; manuals teach snub braking in the correct low gear.
distractorExplanations.d: Gear selection happens before the descent; downshifting after speed builds risks a missed shift and a runaway.

options.a: Steer hard against the swing to snap it straight
options.b: Reduce threats; do not worsen with panic inputs
options.c: Use the hand valve to pull it in line
options.d: Accelerate briefly to stretch the trailers straight

distractorExplanations.a: Hard counter-steering is amplified at the rear trailer and can roll it; use smooth, measured corrections instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Trailer-only braking can lock the rear trailer's wheels and worsen the swing; easing off the brakes helps regain traction.
distractorExplanations.d: Accelerating raises speed and swing energy; the trained response is to ease off, not to power through the swing.

options.a: Hold speed steady
options.b: Speed up to clear the gusts sooner
options.c: Reduce speed further
options.d: Use high beams to watch the trailer

distractorExplanations.a: Crosswind on a light rear trailer at night calls for lower speed; holding speed leaves the swing and rollover risk unchanged.
distractorExplanations.b: Higher speed increases wind-induced sway and rollover energy; slowing down is the correct response.
distractorExplanations.d: High beams light the road ahead, not the trailer; they also blind oncoming drivers and do nothing to reduce swing.

options.a: Acceptable with flashers on
options.b: Safe with one spotter at the rear
options.c: Extremely hazardous—avoid/reposition
options.d: Allowed if traffic is light at night

distractorExplanations.a: Flashers warn others but do not make backing a double into traffic safe; plan routes so no backing is needed.
distractorExplanations.b: A spotter helps in yards, but a double cannot be reliably backed into live traffic; reposition the rig instead.
distractorExplanations.d: Light traffic and darkness reduce visibility further; backing doubles into traffic stays hazardous at any hour.

options.a: Hours-of-service log entries
options.b: Turns, bridges, restrictions
options.c: Bridge heights and weight limits
options.d: IFTA fuel-tax reporting

distractorExplanations.a: HOS logs record duty time, not vehicle length; overall length matters for turns, bridges and length-restricted routes.
distractorExplanations.c: Bridge clearance depends on vehicle height and weight postings on gross weight; overall length governs turns and route restrictions.
distractorExplanations.d: IFTA reports miles and fuel by jurisdiction; overall length matters for turning space and length-restricted routes.

options.a: Cause rear lock/swing
options.b: Mute low-air alarm
options.c: Raise the governor cut-out
options.d: Shorten stopping distance

distractorExplanations.b: The low-air warning responds to reservoir pressure (about 60 psi), not to how braking force is shared between axles.
distractorExplanations.c: Governor cut-out (about 125 psi) is set by the compressor governor and is unrelated to brake proportioning.
distractorExplanations.d: Unbalanced braking makes some wheels lock while others under-brake, lengthening stops and causing trailer swing.

options.a: Check the tractor tires only
options.b: Continue and inspect at the next stop
options.c: Inspect tires/axles/coupling
options.d: Watch the mirror for wobble

distractorExplanations.a: The rear trailer took the impact; its tires, wheels, axle and the dolly coupling must be inspected, not just the tractor.
distractorExplanations.b: Curb strikes can cut tires or bend axles; inspect before continuing, since the damage can fail at highway speed.
distractorExplanations.d: Mirror checks miss cut sidewalls, bent rims and damaged coupling parts; stop and inspect them physically.

options.a: Use the horn as the stop signal
options.b: Agree on signals before moving
options.c: Keep moving if the spotter leaves view
options.d: Agree on signals once you start backing

distractorExplanations.a: Horn signals can be misheard over yard noise; agree on hand signals in advance and stop whenever you lose sight of the spotter.
distractorExplanations.c: Losing sight of the spotter means stopping at once until visual contact is restored, not continuing the move.
distractorExplanations.d: Signals are agreed before any movement begins; working them out mid-maneuver invites misread commands.

options.a: Usable at reduced speed
options.b: Usable if logged on the DVIR
options.c: Usable to the nearest terminal
options.d: Out of service until fixed

distractorExplanations.a: Lower speed does not make unsafe equipment legal; defective equipment stays out of service until it is repaired.
distractorExplanations.b: Listing a defect on the DVIR does not authorize driving; the defect must be repaired and certified first.
distractorExplanations.c: Unsafe equipment is not driven to a terminal under its own power; it is repaired on site or towed.
